title: How to Deliver Tough Feedback in as Little as 5 Minutes
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain begins with a personal failure: he avoided raising a star performer's slipping performance until the damage was done, and she was hurt that he had not spoken sooner. From this he argues that avoiding tough feedback lets small problems snowball, erodes the team's trust in the leader, and burdens the leader with guilt. He then presents a five-step, five-minute framework: prepare with specific observations, state the problem factually, explain its impact, invite the person's input, and agree on a concrete action plan together. Throughout he stresses keeping feedback about behavior rather than the person and delivering it soon after the behavior is observed. The piece closes by addressing fear of confrontation, framing feedback as help rather than harm, a skill that improves with practice, and something that requires honesty rather than perfect words.
points: Jain's own delay in addressing a star performer's decline left her blindsided and hurt, illustrating the cost of avoidance.
Avoided feedback lets small problems grow, makes the team question whether the leader knows or cares, and burdens the leader with guilt.
The five-minute framework runs prepare, state the problem, explain the impact, invite input, and solve together, keeping focus on behavior rather than the person.
Inviting the other person's input often surfaces context, as when a manager discovered an employee's lateness stemmed from morning childcare challenges.
quotes: I remember one time, many years ago, when one of my team members started showing signs of a decline in performance. She was one of my star performers, so at first, I just chose to ignore it and brushed it off. “Maybe it’s just a bad week,” I told myself.
The missed deadlines started piling up, and the team began feeling the strain. By the time I finally mustered up the courage to talk to her, it was too late. The damage was done.

Here’s the thing: tough feedback doesn’t have to feel like a battle. It doesn’t need to be awkward, or overly polished. With a simple approach, you can deliver it in five minutes flat—and come out stronger for it.
Your team loses trust in you. They may not ask you, but they will definitely wonder why you’re not stepping in. They will wonder if you even know, or care.
Ask them what happened. Keep your tone neutral, and empathetic. The goal is to understand, not accuse.

A manager I know used this exact framework with an employee who was often late. Within five minutes, they uncovered the reason: the employee had childcare challenges in the mornings. Together, they adjusted work hours slightly.
You don’t need the “perfect” words. What matters is honesty and respect. What matters is that you have the conversation.
